clue.text: Account with money? Grand, though not really in the post

parts.note: ac is the standing abbreviation for an account, as on a bank statement
tin is old British slang for cash
a grand is a thousand pounds, shortened to its first letter

explanation.surface: A brisk tot-up of somebody's finances, with a payment apparently still sitting in the mail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the post' reads as the mail and means holding a job, and 'not really' is the word that turns the job into a temporary stand-in.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone acting head or acting captain fills the post only for now, deputising rather than truly holding it.

clue.text: Vandalised phone-box: one's beginning to anticipate anti-foreigner sentiment

indicators.note: Vandals wreck what they get hold of, and a wrecked word keeps none of its letters where the setter put them.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters; the hyphen counts for nothing
one written as the single figure I, the way a lone person is

indicators.note: What stands at the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so just one character comes from the word that follows.

parts.note: the first letter of anticipate

explanation.surface: A smashed-up phone box, and somebody starting to see what is coming next.
explanation.walkthrough: Hearing 'one's' as the letter I is what makes the arithmetic work: the phone-box supplies eight letters and the sentiment needs ten.
explanation.definitionFit: Xenophobia is Greek for fear of the stranger, and English uses it for settled hostility towards foreigners rather than for any private phobia.

clue.text: Police vehicle: evidence of damage seen around one in four?

indicators.note: Going around something means passing outside it on both sides, so the word named first splits open and encloses the next one.

parts.note: a scar is the mark left where damage can still be seen
a quad is one of four children born together

explanation.surface: A battered motor is looked over, as though damage showed on one vehicle in every four.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon is doing the work of an equals sign, and 'one in four' is a person rather than a proportion — quads arrive four at a time.
explanation.definitionFit: A squad car is the patrol car a police squad rides in, so the phrase names it by the job it does.

clue.text: Damsel embracing another, ultimately a hard thing to bear

indicators.note: the damsel word is embracing, holding inside it, the next letter

parts.note: a wench is an old word for a girl or young woman, like damsel

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of the word

parts.note: the word whose last letter is taken

explanation.surface: A damsel hugging another girl, a hard parting to bear.
explanation.walkthrough: R, the last letter of another, goes inside WENCH.
explanation.definitionFit: A wrench is a painful parting or emotional upheaval, something hard to endure.

clue.text: Retract intelligence on origin of huge lottery

parts.note: wit is quickness of mind, intelligence

indicators.note: The origin of a word is the point it starts from, so only the opening letter of what comes next is used.

parts.note: the first letter of huge
a lottery is a draw, the pulling out of winning numbers

explanation.surface: Secret intelligence and an enormous prize draw, with somebody told to take it all back.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' means sitting on top of, so the pieces stack down the column in the order the clue names them.
explanation.definitionFit: To withdraw a remark is to retract it, take it back — the verb of statements rather than of money or troops.

clue.text: Minor yet somehow a great crime

indicators.note: The word admits the route from one to the other is unstated, and letters that travel by no stated route arrive in a fresh order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: An offence being brushed aside as small when it was anything but.
explanation.walkthrough: Enormity is the most misused word in the language: it means monstrous wickedness, not great size, and 'Minor' is teasing that very confusion.
explanation.definitionFit: Enormity is an outrage or atrocity — moral monstrousness rather than mere hugeness — so a great crime is its strict sense.

clue.text: Teaching degree? Resign about student coverage at night

definitions.note: 'Coverage' is an abstract noun while the answer is a solid object; the setter is using it for the thing that provides the covering.

parts.note: a BEd is a Bachelor of Education, the usual British teaching qualification

indicators.note: 'About' in a clue means round the outside, so the word before it opens up and takes the piece named after it inside.

parts.note: to quit a post is to resign from it
L is the learner plate a British driver displays, and crosswords use it for any student

explanation.surface: A teacher walks out over a student, and the conversation turns to what happens after dark.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags 'Teaching degree' as one example among several, which is the setter admitting that the letters come from a particular qualification.
explanation.definitionFit: A bed-quilt is the padded cover spread over a bed, so it is what does the covering when you are asleep.

clue.text: Flag of European country getting trimmed

indicators.note: Trimming takes a bit off the end of something, so the last letter is snipped from the word before it.

parts.note: belonging to Ireland = Irish
that word loses its final H

explanation.surface: A national flag described as being cut down to size.
explanation.walkthrough: Flag is a genuine plant name — the yellow flag that grows at the water's edge is a wild iris — so a flower is being defined by a flower's other name.
explanation.definitionFit: Flag is the common English name of the wild iris, so the definition is one plant name standing in for another.

clue.text: Component of extravagant oyster trifles

indicators.note: A component sits inside the thing it belongs to, which is where these letters are — already lying in the words that follow.

parts.note: the end of the first word runs straight on into the start of the second, with no break in the letters

explanation.surface: The ingredient list for a lavish dessert, oysters and all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trifles' is doing the defining as a noun meaning things of no consequence, while the surface has you tasting pudding.
explanation.definitionFit: Trifles are things of no importance, and toys carries that dismissive sense — a plaything, something nobody need take seriously.

clue.text: Discussion item admitting river forms line on map

indicators.note: To admit a visitor is to let them in, so the word doing the admitting takes the next letter inside itself.

parts.note: a topic is an item up for discussion
R is the map-maker's abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: An agenda point that lets a river into the conversation.
explanation.walkthrough: Cancer and Capricorn are the two of them printed across every globe, which is what makes a singular definition fair here.
explanation.definitionFit: A tropic is one of the two latitude circles ruled across an atlas page, so it is literally a line drawn on a map.

clue.text: Pub and brewery finally introducing it in the area

indicators.note: to introduce is to put in, so it goes inside the pub and brewery letters

parts.note: a local is one's nearby pub

indicators.note: finally points to the final letter of the word

parts.note: the word whose last letter is taken

explanation.surface: A pub and a brewery bringing a new beer into the neighbourhood.
explanation.walkthrough: LOCAL plus Y, the last letter of brewery, gives LOCALY; 'introducing' puts IT inside, before the Y.
explanation.definitionFit: A locality is a particular neighbourhood or district, an area.

clue.text: Protest followed by explicit part of the population

indicators.note: Saying one thing is followed by another fixes their order, so the piece named first is written down first.

parts.note: a demo is a demonstration, a public protest
graphic detail is explicit detail

explanation.surface: A march through the streets, and then something described in unsparing detail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Explicit' is aiming you at rude pictures, and the answer is the flat marketing noun for a slice of people picked out by age or income.
explanation.definitionFit: A demographic is a segment of a population sharing some characteristic, the sense advertisers use when they talk about reaching one.

clue.text: Run a diocese, at first followed by member of clergy

indicators.note: followed by means the clergy piece comes after the letters before it
at first means only the opening letter of diocese is wanted here

parts.note: the word whose opening letter is taken
a minister is a member of the clergy

explanation.surface: A bishop runs a diocese, with a vicar coming along behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at first' takes only the D of diocese, and 'followed by' puts the clergyman after A and D. 'Run' is a verb here, as in running a business, not a dash or a ladder in a stocking.
explanation.definitionFit: To administer an organisation is to manage or direct it, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Was home, excited to support good TV programme?

indicators.note: in a down answer a piece that supports another sits below it
excited letters are stirred up into a new order

parts.note: the letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone at home, excited to watch and cheer on a good television show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'excited' rearranges WASHOME into AMESHOW, which supports, sits under, the G for good.
explanation.definitionFit: A game show is a broadcast in which contestants play games for prizes, one kind of television entertainment.

clue.text: Popular time to go round a French swamp

indicators.note: Going round something means passing outside it, so the pieces already assembled close over the word named next.

parts.note: what is popular is in, in fashion
a date is a fixed time in the calendar
un is the French for a

explanation.surface: A fashionable season for touring a French marsh.
explanation.walkthrough: French words are fair game in British cryptics, and 'a French' is the standard way of asking for one; the definition is the verb, to flood.
explanation.definitionFit: To inundate is to flood or overwhelm, and swamp as a verb means precisely that — swamped with letters, inundated with them.

clue.text: Opposite of Caesar, J?

parts.note: Mark Antony was Julius Caesar's ally and then the man set against his heirs
the clue writes Caesar as a register would, surname then initial, so the rival gets his initial too — M for Mark

explanation.surface: A history quiz question: who stood on the other side from Julius Caesar?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caesar, J' is the surname-then-initial form the joke depends on: his opponent set down the same way is Antony, M, which is also an ordinary English word.
explanation.definitionFit: An antonym is a word of contrary meaning — hot to cold — so the noun 'Opposite' is its everyday equivalent.

clue.text: Decline instantly: one's worried over dodgy bar

indicators.note: in a down answer, a piece over another comes above it
worried letters are fretted about, shaken into a new order

parts.note: the letters rearranged
a dive is a disreputable, dodgy bar or club

explanation.surface: Someone anxious about a seedy bar, who instantly turns down the invitation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'worried' rearranges ONES into NOSE, which sits over DIVE.
explanation.definitionFit: To nosedive is to fall or drop suddenly and steeply, a sharp and sudden decline.

clue.text: Reader initially gripped by book once more — it's a good buy

parts.note: b is the standard abbreviation for book

indicators.note: A word taken initially yields the letter it opens with, so one character comes from the noun before it.
To be gripped is to be held fast inside something's grasp, so that letter lands within the pieces named afterwards.

parts.note: once more = again
the first letter of Reader

explanation.surface: Someone reading is caught up in a book for a second time, and it was cheap at the price.
explanation.walkthrough: The insertion lands inside a two-piece assembly rather than inside one word, which is why the seam is so hard to see; the dash marks where the definition starts.
explanation.definitionFit: A bargain is something bought for less than it is worth, so a good buy names it from the buyer's side of the counter.

clue.text: Person again troubled resident of city-state

indicators.note: Someone troubled is unsettled, and unsettled letters do not stay in the order the clue handed them over in.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters

explanation.surface: Somebody is bothered all over again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Again' is passing itself off as an ordinary adverb, which is what keeps the fodder from looking like fodder — those five letters are working, not commenting.
explanation.definitionFit: Singapore is a city that is also a sovereign country, so one of its nationals is exactly a resident of a city-state.

clue.text: Party, upsetting for us, stinks

indicators.note: in a down clue upsetting turns the word upside down, so it is read from the bottom up

parts.note: a do is a party
something for us is ours

explanation.surface: A party that upsets us and leaves a bad smell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upsetting' reverses DO into OD, followed by OURS.
explanation.definitionFit: Odours are smells, and stinks are bad smells, so the plural nouns match.

clue.text: Material to support attack in backgammon

indicators.note: The smallest of signposts: it says the letters are inside the word that follows, not made from it.

parts.note: four consecutive letters sit in the word, starting from its fifth

explanation.surface: A board game, and the supplies an attacking player needs.
explanation.walkthrough: Backgammon is doing double duty — a game in the surface, a hiding place in the wordplay — and that one-letter 'in' is the only signpost you get.
explanation.definitionFit: Ammo is the clipped everyday form of ammunition, the material an attack is supplied with, and it carries the figurative sense too.

clue.text: Limits to general use adhesive

indicators.note: The limits of a word are its two edges, so the opening and closing letters of each word named next are taken.

parts.note: the two edges of g-enera-l
the two edges of u-s-e

explanation.surface: Restrictions written into what everybody is allowed to use.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Limits to general use' reads as small print on a licence, and that entirely plausible sentence is what hides an instruction inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Adhesive is the class name for anything that sticks things together, and glue is the everyday member of that class.

clue.text: Song-writer seldom getting confused with it

indicators.note: Something confused is muddled up, and muddled letters settle into an order nobody chose.

parts.note: anagram fodder, six letters
two more letters joined to the fodder

explanation.surface: A composer who is hardly ever mistaken for anything else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting confused with it' reads as praise for a distinctive musician, and it is the instruction plus the last two letters it works on.
explanation.definitionFit: A melodist is a writer of melodies, the tunes that carry songs, so the job title and the definition name the same trade.

clue.text: Religious writer to ridicule leaders of Unitarian Adventists

parts.note: to josh is to tease or make fun of

indicators.note: the leaders of words are their first letters

parts.note: the two words whose first letters are taken

explanation.surface: A religious author setting out to mock the heads of two church groups.
explanation.walkthrough: JOSH is followed by U and A, the first letters of Unitarian and Adventists.
explanation.definitionFit: The Old Testament Book of Joshua was traditionally credited to Joshua himself as its author.

clue.text: Completed challenge with summary

parts.note: when something is over it is finished
to vie is to compete, to challenge for something
w/ is the standard shorthand for with

explanation.surface: A challenge has been finished, and written up in brief.
explanation.walkthrough: The smoothest word in the sentence is the one carrying a letter: 'with' looks like joinery holding two halves together and is a piece of the build.
explanation.definitionFit: An overview is a broad account with the detail left out, which is what a summary gives you — the whole thing seen from above.

clue.text: Items often furrowed before end of intense look over the shelves?

indicators.note: Standing before something means coming in front of it, which fixes which of the two pieces is written first.

parts.note: brows are what you furrow when you frown

indicators.note: The end of a word is its closing letter, and that single character is all this takes from the word after it.

parts.note: the last letter of intense

explanation.surface: A deep frown, held right up to the end of an intense stare.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that shelves are only one place you can do this, which is what lets a whole phrase stand as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To browse is to scan goods or books at leisure with nothing particular in mind, and drifting along a shelf is the everyday instance of it.
